extracted.intended_audience: researchers, educators, and child-development practitioners (preschool/primary school)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical study applying McGhee's humor development stages to measure children's laughter responses to video stimuli; aimed at understanding age-related humor appreciation and informing educational practice. Includes methods for stimulus design, observation, recording, coding, and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee Stage 0 — laughter without humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage zero, or laughter without humor (first 6 months): babies often laugh with no humor being present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infants' laughter may occur without perceivable incongruity or cognitive appreciation; stage excluded from video stimuli because laughter contains no humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee Stage 1 — laughter at attachment figure
rubrics_metrics.description: First stage, laughter at the attachment figure (6 months-12/15 months): children laugh at unfamiliar actions of their parents/attachment figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage 1 examples were not included in the video because laughter is directed at attachment figures rather than to conceptual incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee Stage 2 — inconsistent behavior towards objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 2 (12/15 months – 3/4/5 years): the child enjoys using familiar objects in unusual and inappropriate ways (e.g., putting a plastic container on the head as a hat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early examples of humor production; video included at least two scenes representing this stage (example: child puts blue plastic container on head saying 'Let me put on my hat first'). Measure laughter response to such object-based incongruities.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee Stage 3 — misnaming objects/events/people
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 3 (2-3/4 years): children start playing with words, calling objects by wrong names (e.g., taking a toy rabbit and saying 'Oh, a toy monkey').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detecting and coding laughter to verbal misnaming; included in video stimuli and observation items.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee Stage 4 — conceptual incongruity (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 4 (3-5 years) — conceptual incongruity, divided into subcategories: playing with sounds, combining meaningless and real words, distorting object/animal/person attributes, and opposite-sex naming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stage has four subcategories (4a–4d); stimuli should represent these subcategories and responses coded separately where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 4a — playing with the sounds of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 4a: playing with the sounds of words (not their meanings) — children adapt to and play with word sounds themselves (example: 'Ice, rice, spice').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sound-play examples in stimuli; observe laughter elicited by phonetic play rather than semantic mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 4b — combination of meaningless and real words
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 4b: combination of meaningless and real words — children put words together in absurd ways even though they know they are wrong (example: 'a huge book pudding over toy soup').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include absurd word-combination scenes and record whether children laugh at semantic absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 4c — objects distorting characteristics of people/animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 4c: distorting characteristics — adding, deleting, changing size/color/shape of known things; children laugh at inconsistent/impossible behaviors (examples: dog meows, upside-down umbrella, car missing wheel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual/behavioral distortions in stimuli; visual incongruities can be especially salient for this subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 4d — opposite-sex naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 4d: opposite-sex naming — children find it amusing when others are called by a name associated with the opposite sex (example: mother says to son 'Fatma').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include naming incongruities; consider social/cultural naming conventions when designing stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee Stage 5 — riddles and jokes (multiple meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 5 (6/7-10/11): comprehension of jokes and riddles featuring double meanings or ambiguity (example: pizza cut into 4 vs 8 pieces 'I'm on a diet, so 8 pieces would be too much').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stimuli for stage 5 require higher cognitive skill and familiarity with multiple-meaning language; expect stronger responses in older children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as necessary condition for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand and appreciate humor, an individual must have a basic understanding of how situations and concepts should be, providing a frame of reference for recognizing incongruity; dissonance/perception of inconsistency is necessary for humor to occur (McGhee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessments or educational humor so that the child has enough cognitive mastery of the expected pattern to perceive the deviation; without this frame, incongruity will not be appreciated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant incongruity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a pleasant incongruity for laughter to occur; children need to be able to 'solve' the incongruity — otherwise humor is not appreciated (citing Morreal, Loizou).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incongruity that is confusing, threatening, or violates real-world expectations disastrously; aim for solvable, benign violations when eliciting laughter or designing educational humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design: single screening model
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a single screening model to determine the formation of variables one by one or based on quantity (Karasar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for cross-sectional descriptive work measuring responses by age group; not longitudinal — consider model limitations when generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus construction and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a scripted video representing McGhee stages with at least two scenes per stage; consult developmental psychology and child development experts to confirm scenes represent stages; make technical and content adjustments per expert feedback; consult music education expert for appropriate background music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure scenes form a harmonious composition, obtain expert validation both pre- and post-production, and adjust stimuli accordingly to maximize representativeness and cultural appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation instrument: semi-structured observation form
rubrics_metrics.description: List video scenes in writing with space for notes about children's laughter responses; include child's code, age, date, time, scene items, first viewing laugh/no laugh, second viewing laugh/no laugh; each scene treated as an item (27 items total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured fields to capture binary laugh/no laugh per scene and space for qualitative notes; use unique codes to preserve anonymity during coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording protocol: video record children for later coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Record children with a laptop camera from entry to exit; do not mark observation forms live; use recordings to fill observation forms later. Use a research diary for situations not captured on the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Video recording allows repeated, careful coding and reduces observer bias; keep detailed research-diary notes to supplement coded data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and assent procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain written parental consent; inform parents at meetings about scope and aim; ask children whether they want to participate and include only willing children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure voluntary participation and written consent for minors; document consent procedures in methods and ethics statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewing/session protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct sessions in a quiet room with minimal distractions; groups of three children, seated one meter from a 13.3-inch laptop screen; allow a second viewing on request to account for attention; children may opt out of second viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize viewing conditions (distance, group size, equipment) to reduce extraneous variability; allow repeated viewing when necessary to capture responses from children who were inattentive initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding rule: laugh/no laugh per scene and combining viewings
rubrics_metrics.description: Record children's reactions to each scene as 'laugh' or 'no laugh' regardless of whether it occurred on the first or second viewing; combine the two monitoring forms for each child into a single response per stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use binary coding for presence/absence of laughter at the scene level and aggregate across viewings when analyzing stage-level responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data analysis methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive analyses and content analyses to analyze research data; in this study, descriptive analysis assessed whether children laughed at scenes according to McGhee stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptive statistics to compare laughter rates by age and stage; use content analysis for qualitative notes and research-diary entries to supplement quantitative findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and reliability practices (Merriam recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase validity and reliability by using multiple researchers, multiple data sources and collection methods, conducting expert interviews/discussions about process and findings, keeping detailed records of decisions and environment, and deliberately creating diversity in the selection of the working group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement triangulation, expert consultation, thick description, audit trails, and purposeful sampling diversity to strengthen qualitative and mixed-methods research credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational practice guideline: use age-appropriate humor and visual aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Adults (parents, teachers) should use examples of humor appropriate for children's developmental characteristics and organize the physical environment with visual aids such as photographs, images, and cartoons that incorporate age-appropriate humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor humorous content to the child's McGhee stage; incorporate visual humor and age-suited jokes into classroom materials to build rapport and support development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher training and implementation capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers find humor necessary in preschool education but need knowledge and experience in planning and implementing activities that support humor; the use of humor in education is a skill that can be learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide professional development to help educators plan, accept, and facilitate child-specific humor; encourage acceptance of children's humor forms in classrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for future research (sampling and design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replicate with larger, culturally diverse samples; consider longitudinal survey models to track individuals over time; use interviews especially for age groups (e.g., 7-year-olds) showing atypical responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger and longitudinal designs increase generalizability and understanding of developmental trajectories; interviews can elucidate reasons behind age-specific laughter patterns.
